Prealgebra · Lesson 5.5

Repeating Decimals

Solve this lesson →All lessons

1331​ can never stop, because 33 is neither 22 nor 55. Its digits run forever, but they are not random. They fall into a loop, and the remainders in long division are what force that loop.

Problem
Long-divide 1÷31÷3. At each step the remainder decides the next digit. What number is the remainder at the end of every step?
Show a hint
  • Don't watch the quotient digit, watch what is left over after you subtract. Each step you have some number, you take away the biggest multiple of 33 you can, and a small leftover stays behind. Write down that leftover for the first two or three steps and see if it changes.
  • On step one you compute 10−9=110−9=1. On step two you pull down a zero to make 1010 again, and 10−9=110−9=1. The leftover after subtracting is the same single digit every single time. Type that digit.
Show the full solution
Bring down a zero and divide. 10÷310÷3 gives digit 33 with 10−9=110−9=1 left over. Bring down another zero and 10÷310÷3 gives 33 again with 11 left over. The remainder at the end of every step is 11​. Since that leftover is the number we started with, the step copies itself forever, which is why 13=0.3‾31​=0.3.
Problem
Long-dividing 1÷71÷7 cycles through remainders 1,3,2,6,4,51,3,2,6,4,5 before 11 returns, giving 17=0.142857‾71​=0.142857. How many digits are in the repeating block?
Show a hint
  • Only 00 through 66 can ever be a remainder, and 00 would stop the decimal. So while it keeps going, every remainder is one of 1,2,3,4,5,61,2,3,4,5,6. The block repeats once a remainder returns, so the longest a block can run before looping is exactly the number of different remainders that show up.
  • List the remainders in order until one comes back. They are 1,3,2,6,4,51,3,2,6,4,5, and then 11 appears again. Count how many remainders you went through before that first repeat. That count is the length of the repeating block.
Show the full solution
Follow the remainders. 10÷710÷7 gives 11 remainder 33, then 30÷730÷7 gives 44 remainder 22, then 20÷720÷7 gives 22 remainder 66, then 60÷760÷7 gives 88 remainder 44, then 40÷740÷7 gives 55 remainder 55, then 50÷750÷7 gives 77 remainder 11. The starting remainder is back after six steps, so the block is 66​ digits long, namely 142857142857. A block can never run longer than the count of available nonzero remainders, and here all six of 11 through 66 get used.
Key idea
Why decimals repeat. Long division produces each digit from a remainder, and it ends only when a remainder is 00. Every remainder is smaller than the divisor bb, so there are at most b−1b−1 possible nonzero remainders. If no remainder is ever 00, some remainder has to repeat, and from that step on every step repeats an earlier one, so the digits repeat in a block of fixed length. That is why 13=0.3‾31​=0.3 and 17=0.142857‾71​=0.142857. The decimal of a fraction always either terminates or repeats.
Problem
In 16=0.16‾61​=0.16, only the 66 repeats. How many digits come before the repeating block begins, meaning how many are not under the bar?
Show a hint
  • Write out the decimal with the bar in the right place. In 0.16‾0.16, the bar covers the looping part. Everything to the left of where the bar starts is the non-repeating head. Just count those digits.
  • The repeating block is the 66, and the bar starts right at it. The only digit sitting before the bar is the 11. So count the digits before the loop begins.
Show the full solution
Divide 11 by 66. 10÷6=110÷6=1 remainder 44, so the first digit is 11. Then 40÷6=640÷6=6 remainder 44, the same remainder, so the 66 repeats from there. That gives 16=0.16‾61​=0.16, and only 11​ digit sits outside the bar. The head comes from the 22 in 6=2×36=2×3. One factor of 22 buys one settling digit, and the 33 makes the loop.
Problem
The long division 1÷111÷11 gives 111=0.09‾111​=0.09. The bar covers both the 00 and the 99. How many digits are in the repeating block? Give the period.
Show a hint
  • The period is just a count. Look at the block sitting under the bar in 0.09‾0.09 and count its digits, including the leading zero.
  • The block is 0909. Count its digits one at a time. There is a 00, and there is a 99. That is two digits.
Show the full solution
10÷11=010÷11=0 remainder 1010, so the first digit after the point is 00. Then 100÷11=9100÷11=9 remainder 11, which is the remainder we began with, so the digits cycle as 0,9,0,9,…0,9,0,9,… and 111=0.09‾111​=0.09. The block 0909 has 22​ digits. Keep that leading zero, since 0.9‾0.9 is a completely different number.
Problem
Long division gives 112=0.083‾121​=0.083. What is the repeating block? Type the digit or digits under the bar.
Show a hint
  • The repeating block is the part that keeps coming back once the digits settle into their loop. The 00 and the 88 at the front each happen only once, so neither of them is part of the loop. Watch for the moment a remainder shows up a second time, because that is exactly when the repetition kicks in.
  • Carry the division out to 0.0833333…0.0833333…. The remainder 44 appears, gives the digit 33, and then comes back as the remainder again, so the same step repeats and you keep writing 33. Only the 33 sits under the bar, so 112=0.083‾121​=0.083.
Show the full solution
Divide 11 by 1212. 10÷12=010÷12=0 remainder 1010, then 100÷12=8100÷12=8 remainder 44, then 40÷12=340÷12=3 remainder 44. Remainder 44 has come back, so that step repeats forever and 112=0.083‾121​=0.083. The block under the bar is 33​. The head 0808 is two digits because 12=22×312=22×3 carries two factors of 22, and the 33 is what loops.
Problem
Which of 116161​, 120201​, 125251​, 115151​ repeats? Factor each denominator and apply the 22s-and-55s test. Give the denominator.
Show a hint
  • Break each denominator into primes. 16=2416=24, 20=22×520=22×5, 25=5225=52, and 15=3×515=3×5. The terminating ones use only the "friendly" primes 22 and 55. Look for the denominator that has a different prime.
  • Three of the denominators are made purely of 22s and 55s, so those three terminate. Only 15=3×515=3×5 carries a prime that is neither 22 nor 55. That stray factor of 33 is what forces the digits to repeat, so the answer is its denominator.
Show the full solution
Factor the four denominators. 16=2416=24, 20=22×520=22×5, 25=5225=52, and 15=3×515=3×5. The first three are built only from 22s and 55s, so they terminate at 0.06250.0625, 0.050.05, and 0.040.04. Only 1515 carries a 33, and 115=0.06‾151​=0.06, so the denominator is 1515​. Only 22 and 55 divide a power of ten, so any other prime can never be scaled away and the remainders cycle instead of reaching 00.
Key idea
Predicting the decimal from the denominator. Factor the denominator of a fraction in lowest terms and you can predict its decimal without dividing. Call 22 and 55 the stopping primes and every other prime a looping prime. A denominator built only from 22s and 55s gives a terminating decimal. With no 22s or 55s, the decimal repeats from the first digit. With both kinds of prime, the decimal has a non-repeating part whose length is the larger stopping-prime count, then a part that repeats forever.

So far we have gone from a fraction to its repeating decimal. The trip back works too. Multiply by a power of ten to make a second copy of the same endless tail, subtract so the two tails cancel, and the infinite decimal collapses into an ordinary fraction.

Problem
Let x=0.7‾x=0.7. Multiply by 1010 to get 10x=7.7‾10x=7.7. The tails of 77s cancel when you subtract: 9x=79x=7. Write 0.7‾0.7 as a fraction in lowest terms.
Show a hint
  • You built two equations, x=0.7777…x=0.7777… and 10x=7.7777…10x=7.7777…. Stack the second over the first and subtract straight down. On the left you get 10x−x10x−x. On the right, the endless 77s line up exactly and wipe each other out, so what whole number is left?
  • Subtracting gives 9x=79x=7. To get xx by itself, divide both sides by 99. That leaves x=79x=97​. Check whether 77 and 99 share any common factor before you call it done.
Show the full solution
Let x=0.7777…x=0.7777…, so 10x=7.7777…10x=7.7777…. Past the decimal point both numbers carry the identical endless string of 77s, so subtracting wipes it out. 10x−x=7.7777…−0.7777…10x−x=7.7777…−0.7777… 9x=79x=7 Divide by 99 to get x=79x=97​, and 77 is prime so nothing reduces. 7/97/9​ Multiplying by 1010 shifts past exactly one block, which is what lines the two tails up.
Problem
Let x=0.12‾x=0.12. Multiply by 100100 to get 100x=12.12‾100x=12.12. Subtracting gives 99x=1299x=12, so x=1299x=9912​. Write 0.12‾0.12 as a fraction in lowest terms.
Show a hint
  • You already know it begins as 12999912​. Now ask the lowest-terms question. What whole number divides both 1212 and 9999 evenly?
  • Both 1212 and 9999 are divisible by 33. Divide the top and the bottom by 33, which gives 12÷3=412÷3=4 and 99÷3=3399÷3=33. Check that 44 and 3333 share no common factor, then you are finished.
Show the full solution
Let x=0.121212…x=0.121212…. The block is two digits, so multiply by 100100. 100x=12.121212…100x=12.121212… The tails match, so subtracting leaves 99x=1299x=12 and x=1299x=9912​. Both parts are divisible by 33. 1299=4339912​=334​ Since 4=2×24=2×2 and 33=3×1133=3×11, this is fully reduced, so 0.12‾=4/330.12=4/33​. The block-over-nines shortcut hands you a correct fraction but rarely a reduced one, so always check.
Problem
Let x=0.9‾x=0.9. Multiply by 1010: 10x=9.9‾10x=9.9. Subtract: 9x=99x=9. Divide by 99. What does 0.9‾0.9 equal?
Show a hint
  • You already did the hard part for 0.7‾0.7. Write x=0.9‾x=0.9 and 10x=9.9‾10x=9.9, then subtract. Trust the cancellation even though the result feels surprising.
  • Subtracting gives 10x−x=9.9‾−0.9‾10x−x=9.9−0.9. The infinite tails of nines are identical, so they vanish and leave 9x=99x=9. Now divide both sides by 9 and read off the single whole number you get.
Show the full solution
Let x=0.9999…x=0.9999…, so 10x=9.9999…10x=9.9999…. After the decimal point both numbers carry the same endless string of nines, so subtracting cancels it. 10x−x=9.9999…−0.9999…10x−x=9.9999…−0.9999… 9x=99x=9 Divide by 99 and x=1x=1​. Nothing was rounded or dropped anywhere in that work, so 0.9‾0.9 is not creeping up toward 11. It is another name for 11.
Problem
Write 0.416‾0.416 as a fraction in lowest terms. Multiply by 1,0001,000 and by 100100, subtract to cancel the 6‾6 tails, then solve and reduce.
Show a hint
  • You want two shifted copies of xx whose decimal tails are identical, so the subtraction wipes the tail out. The repeating part is 0.006‾0.006, sitting two places in. Try sliding the point so one copy stops just before the loop and the other stops just after one block of it.
  • Let x=0.416‾x=0.416. Multiply by 100100 to land just before the loop, 100x=41.6‾=41.666…100x=41.6=41.666…. Multiply by 1,0001,000 to land one block past it, 1,000x=416.6‾=416.666…1,000x=416.6=416.666…. Both end in the same .666….666… tail. Subtract the smaller from the larger and solve for xx, then reduce.
Show the full solution
Let x=0.41666…x=0.41666…. Shift past the head with 100x=41.666…100x=41.666…, then one block further with 1,000x=416.666…1,000x=416.666…. Both end in the same .666….666… tail, so subtracting cancels it. 1,000x−100x=416.666…−41.666…1,000x−100x=416.666…−41.666… 900x=375900x=375 Then x=375900x=900375​, and both share a factor of 7575, since 375=75⋅5375=75⋅5 and 900=75⋅12900=75⋅12. x=5/12x=5/12​ When there is a non-repeating head you need two shifts, one landing just before the loop and one a full block later.
Key idea
Repeating decimals as fractions. Multiply the decimal by the power of ten that shifts it one block, then subtract the original. The repeating parts cancel and leave a plain equation. A decimal repeating from the first digit equals its block over a string of 99s, one 99 per digit. 0.7‾=790.7=97​, 0.12‾=12990.12=9912​, 0.481‾=4819990.481=999481​, then reduce. It also gives 0.9‾=99=10.9=99​=1, exactly 11, since an infinite decimal is one fixed number.
Fun fact
In base 77, the fraction 1771​ would simply be 0.10.1, while 1221​ would repeat. Whether a decimal terminates depends on the base, not the fraction.
Problem
17=0.142857‾71​=0.142857, a block of 66 digits. Divide 50÷650÷6 to find the position within the block. What is the 50th digit after the decimal point?
Show a hint
  • The block 142857142857 is six digits long, so the pattern resets every 66 positions. Every time you pass a full group of 66, you are back at the start of the block. So really you just need to know how far past the last full group position 5050 sits.
  • Divide 5050 by 66. You get 88 full blocks with 22 left over. That remainder of 22 tells you the 5050th digit is the same as the 22nd digit of the block 142857142857. Read off the second digit.
Show the full solution
The block 142857142857 is six digits long, so divide. 50=6×8+250=6×8+2, which puts position 5050 two digits into a fresh block. The second digit of 142857142857 is 44​. Only the remainder picks the digit. The quotient 88 just counts how many full blocks you skipped past.
Key idea
Finding a far digit. The length of the repeating block is called the period. Once you know the block and its period, every digit is determined. A far-off digit depends only on where its position falls inside the block. Divide the position by the period and read the remainder. Remainder 11 means the first digit of the block, remainder 22 the second, and remainder 00 means the last digit. No long division is needed past finding the period.
Problem
Find 0.72‾−0.27‾0.72−0.27 as a single fraction in lowest terms. Convert each to a fraction over 9999, subtract, then reduce.
Show a hint
  • Each of these has a two-digit repeating block, and you found a shortcut for exactly this. A repeating two-digit block sits over 9999. So turn each decimal into a fraction with denominator 9999 before you do anything else.
  • Once both are written over 9999, they share a denominator, so you can subtract the top numbers directly and keep the 9999 underneath. That leaves one fraction. Now reduce it by dividing the top and bottom by their greatest common factor.
Show the full solution
A two-digit block sits over 9999, so 0.72‾=72990.72=9972​ and 0.27‾=27990.27=9927​. The denominators already match, so subtract the numerators. 7299−2799=45999972​−9927​=9945​ Both 4545 and 9999 are divisible by 99, which gives 511115​, and 55 shares no factor with 1111. 5/115/11​ Checking, 511=0.45‾115​=0.45, and 0.7272…0.7272… minus 0.2727…0.2727… does leave 0.4545…0.4545….

Practice these ideas

Practice
Long-divide 2÷32÷3. Each step ends with the same remainder. What single digit repeats forever in the decimal 0.6‾0.6?
Show the solution
Since 33 is bigger than 22, the whole-number part is 00 and the remainder is 22. Then 20÷3=620÷3=6 with remainder 20−18=220−18=2, the remainder we started with, so every step after that prints another 66. That makes 2÷3=0.6‾2÷3=0.6, so the repeating digit is 66​. A returning remainder is exactly what locks a decimal into a loop.
Practice
Long-divide 1÷91÷9. The remainder returns immediately, giving 19=0.1‾91​=0.1. How many digits are in the repeating block? Give the period.
Show the solution
Bring down a zero to get 1010. Then 10÷9=110÷9=1 with remainder 11, the number we started with, so every step writes another 11 and 19=0.1‾91​=0.1. The bar covers a single digit, so the period is 11​.
Practice
Long-divide 1÷111÷11. The remainder returns after two digits, giving 111=0.09‾111​=0.09. Write the repeating block as a digit string, including the leading zero.
Show the solution
Start with remainder 11. Attach a zero to get 1010, and 1111 fits into 1010 zero times, so the first digit is 00 and the remainder is 1010. Attach another zero to get 100100, and 1111 fits 99 times since 9×11=999×11=99, leaving remainder 11 again. The digits cycle as 0,9,0,9,…0,9,0,9,…, so the block is 0909​. The leading zero is part of the block, not decoration.
Practice
5÷6=0.83‾5÷6=0.83. The digit 88 settles before the loop. How many digits come before the repeating block begins?
Show the solution
50÷6=850÷6=8 with remainder 22, so the first decimal digit is 88. Then 20÷6=320÷6=3 with remainder 22 again, so the 33 loops from there and 56=0.83‾65​=0.83. Exactly 11​ digit sits outside the bar. A decimal like this is called eventually repeating, since it settles into its loop after a short run-up instead of right away.
Practice
Long-divide 7÷307÷30 to find 730=0.23‾307​=0.23. The 22 settles first. What single digit is the repeating block?
Show the solution
70÷30=270÷30=2 with remainder 1010, so the first decimal digit is 22. Then 100÷30=3100÷30=3 with remainder 1010, the same remainder, so every later step writes another 33. That gives 730=0.23‾307​=0.23, so the repeating block is 33​. The 22 and the 55 in 3030 produce the one settling digit, and the 33 produces the loop.
Practice
Let x=0.5‾x=0.5. Multiply by 1010: 10x=5.5‾10x=5.5. Subtract: 9x=59x=5. Write 0.5‾0.5 as a fraction in lowest terms.
Show the solution
Let x=0.5555…x=0.5555…, so 10x=5.5555…10x=5.5555…. Both numbers end in the identical endless string of fives, so subtracting cancels the tails and leaves 9x=59x=5. Divide by 99 to get x=59x=95​, and since 9=3×39=3×3 shares nothing with 55, it is already in lowest terms. 5/95/9​
Practice
Using the block-over-nines shortcut, 0.2‾0.2 has a one-digit block, so it equals 2992​. Write 0.2‾0.2 as a fraction in lowest terms.
Show the solution
The block is one digit, so it goes over a single nine, and 0.2‾=290.2=92​. The factors of 22 are 11 and 22, the factors of 99 are 11, 33, and 99, so they share only 11 and the fraction cannot shrink. 2/92/9​ That nine is really 10−110−1. Setting x=0.2‾x=0.2 and subtracting gives 10x−x=9x=210x−x=9x=2.
Practice
The decimal 0.81‾0.81 equals 81999981​. Reduce 81999981​ to lowest terms. What fraction do you get?
Show the solution
A two-digit block sits over 9999, so 0.81‾=81990.81=9981​. The greatest common factor of 8181 and 9999 is 99, since 81=9×981=9×9 and 99=9×1199=9×11. Dividing top and bottom by 99 gives 9/119/11​. Checking, 9÷11=0.818181…9÷11=0.818181…. The block-over-nines shortcut gives a correct value but rarely a reduced one.
Practice
Write 0.045‾0.045 as a fraction in lowest terms. Use 1,000x1,000x and 10x10x to cancel the repeating tails, giving 990x=45990x=45, then reduce.
Show the solution
Let x=0.0454545…x=0.0454545…. Shift three places to land just before a fresh block, 1,000x=45.4545…1,000x=45.4545…, and one place to clear the head zero, 10x=0.4545…10x=0.4545…. Both end in the same .4545….4545… tail, so subtracting gives 990x=45990x=45 and x=45990x=99045​. Both share 4545, since 990=45⋅22990=45⋅22, so x=1/22x=1/22​. The leading zero appears once and never repeats, which is why a single shift will not line the tails up.
Practice
Let x=0.9‾x=0.9. Multiply by 1010: 10x=9.9‾10x=9.9. Subtract and solve. What single whole number does 0.9‾0.9 equal?
Show the solution
Let x=0.9‾x=0.9, so 10x=9.9‾10x=9.9. After the decimal point both carry the identical endless string of nines, so subtracting cancels it and leaves 9x=99x=9. Divide by 99 and x=1x=1​. A second check agrees. 0.1‾=190.1=91​, and nine copies give 99=199​=1 while 9⋅0.1‾=0.9‾9⋅0.1=0.9.
Practice
113=0.076923‾131​=0.076923, a block of 66 digits. Divide 100÷6100÷6 to place the position within the block. What is the 100th digit after the decimal point?
Show the solution
The block 076923076923 is six digits long, so divide. 100=6×16+4100=6×16+4, since 6×16=966×16=96, which puts position 100100 four digits into a fresh block. Reading 076923076923, the 4th digit is 99​. The quotient 1616 only counts the full blocks that went by. The remainder is what picks the digit.
Practice
433=0.12‾334​=0.12, a block of 22 digits. Divide 99÷299÷2 to find the position in the block. What is the 99th digit after the decimal point?
Show the solution
The block 1212 is two digits long, so divide. 99=2×49+199=2×49+1, so position 9999 lands on the first digit of the block, which is 11​. With a block of length 22, odd positions all hold the 11 and even positions all hold the 22, and 9999 is odd.
Practice
Factor each denominator: 8=238=23, 40=23×540=23×5, 50=2×5250=2×52, 24=23×324=23×3. Which denominator contains a prime other than 22 or 55, forcing its decimal to repeat?
Show the solution
Read the factorizations. 8=238=23, 40=23×540=23×5, and 50=2×5250=2×52 use only 22s and 55s, so all three terminate. 24=23×324=23×3 carries a 33, which is neither 22 nor 55, so the repeating denominator is 2424​. Its decimal is 124=0.0416‾241​=0.0416, and that stray 33 is the reason it never ends.
Practice
Find 0.81‾−0.36‾0.81−0.36 as a single fraction in lowest terms. Both two-digit repeaters sit over 9999. Subtract the numerators and reduce.
Show the solution
A two-digit block sits over 9999, so 0.81‾=81990.81=9981​ and 0.36‾=36990.36=9936​. The denominators match, so subtract the numerators. 8199−3699=45999981​−9936​=9945​ Both 4545 and 9999 are divisible by 99, since 45=9×545=9×5 and 99=9×1199=9×11, so the answer is 5/115/11​. Checking, 5÷11=0.45‾5÷11=0.45, exactly the gap between the two decimals.
